newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany to reform taxes without SPD - Schaeuble.
newsitem.headline: Germany to reform taxes without SPD - Schaeuble.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's top tax strategist, exasperated by the opposition Social Democrats' (SPD) delaying tactics, vowed on Wednesday the government would press ahead "step by step" with planned tax reforms.
Wolfgang Schaeuble, parliamentary chief of Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), pinned the blame for a breakdown in cross-party talks firmly on SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine.
Lafontaine has refused to rejoin talks on government plans to cut taxes, which he quit in a recent row over coal subsidies, unless he gets to meet Kohl face-to-face.

"Obviously the vanities of protocol are more important for Oskar Lafontaine that achieving results in the fight against unemployment," Schaeuble wrote in a newspaper column. "We will not accept any further delays."

Schaeuble said that, in addition to a 1998 tax bill already introduced into parliament, the government would soon initiate legislation for 1999 which would implement the lion's share of 30 billion marks ($17.8 billion) of cuts in corporate and income taxes.

"If the SPD wants to return to the negotiating table it is most welcome. But if it continues to gamble on its blockade, it should give up saying that it thinks fighting unemployment is so important," Schaeuble wrote in the article, which was due to be published on Thursday in the Esslinger Zeitung.

The SPD has the power to block tax measures through its control of the upper house of parliament. A failure of the tax talks would force the two sides to try to strike a bargain in parliamentary arbitration later this year.

Schaeuble said the SPD's efforts to create "a climate of confusion and uncertainty" might give its opinion poll ratings a short-term boost, but it would not solve unemployment, running at 4.7 million people, or stimulate job-creating investment.
Earlier, a leader of junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP) said the cross-party talks had failed.
Walter Doering, Baden-Wuerttemberg state finance minister, told the Bild newspaper that the SPD "clearly had no interest in cooperating with the coalition on the tax reforms.

"The economic situation in Germany is so serious that we cannot wait while the SPD plays tactical games. The Bonn coalition must seize the initiative and move the reforms along alone," Doering told Bild.

The SPD on Tuesday blamed Kohl for the failure to get the tax talks going. Chief whip Peter Struck said Kohl did not really want tax reforms, and knew full well the proposals drafted by Finance Minister Theo Waigel were irresponsible.
-- Douglas Busvine, Bonn newsroom, 49-228-26097 150 ($ = 1.685 German Marks)
